did_you_know.text: The word “old” in the Bible can also signal the close of an era; here it shows the main phase of the conquest was nearly finished while Joshua’s leadership continued.
The “five princes of the Philistines” refers to the five coastal city-states (like Ashkelon, Ashdod and Gath). Gath is also named in the Bible as the hometown of the giant Goliath.
Sidon was one of the ancient Mediterranean Phoenician cities — its mention points to the coastal, maritime trade connections with Canaan.
Mount Hermon and Hamath form a prominent northern boundary in the Bible; Hamath is identified with an ancient site around the modern city of Hama in Syria.
The highlands were hard to conquer and often sheltered local populations — this verse reflects the practical difficulty of controlling mountainous regions.
The land is allotted to nine tribes plus half of Manasseh — so not all Israelite tribes received a continuous territory in the same way.
The kingdom of Og in Bashan is mentioned; Og is counted among the Rephaim — a group sometimes depicted as giants — and his defeat is linked to Moses’ military campaigns.
Geshur and Maacah were not completely driven out and remained within Israel’s borders — Geshur is also associated in later narratives with David’s family.
The Levites did not receive a contiguous inheritance because their role was religious; instead they lived in scattered towns and served the people and the sanctuary.
Balaam son of Beor, earlier depicted as a prophet and famous for the talking donkey episode, was killed by the Israelites.
In Bashan sixty towns are named as Jair’s settlements — indicating a cluster of local villages or towns that bore the name of a local leader (Jair).
